faqSchema.source:
No. The intra-oral scanner simply passes over the teeth. A CBCT scan involves sitting or standing still for under a minute and nothing touches you.

For most restorative work a well-taken digital scan gives an excellent result and removes the discomfort of putty. In a small number of situations a conventional impression remains the better option, and we will use one where that is the case.

Because some questions cannot be answered in two dimensions — bone width, nerve position, root anatomy. Where a standard X-ray answers the question, we take one instead.

It uses a higher dose than a standard dental X-ray, which is why it is taken only where clinically justified. The reason for any scan is explained to you first.

Tell us before any imaging. Non-urgent radiography is generally deferred during pregnancy, and we will discuss timing with you.

Yes. Records can be provided to you or sent to another practitioner on request.

fields.label: Main heading
fields.value: Better information, and no tray of putty.

fields.label: Introduction
fields.value: Two pieces of technology do most of the work behind the scenes here: an intra-oral scanner and a 3D cone beam scanner. Neither is treatment in itself. Both make treatment easier to plan, more accurate to deliver and, in the case of the scanner, considerably more comfortable to sit through.

fields.label: Small heading
fields.value: Digital intra-oral scanning

fields.label: Paragraph
fields.value: A small handheld wand is passed over your teeth and builds a three-dimensional model on screen in a few minutes. For most patients it replaces the tray of impression putty entirely.

fields.label: Paragraph
fields.value: If you have a strong gag reflex, that alone is worth a great deal. There is no material setting in your mouth, no tray pressing against the palate, and the scan can be paused at any point.

fields.label: Paragraph
fields.value: Accuracy is the other benefit. A conventional impression can distort slightly as the material sets or as it travels to the laboratory. A digital scan is sent electronically without a physical model in between, which removes those variables from the fit of crowns, bridges, dentures, night guards and mouthguards.

fields.label: Paragraph
fields.value: It also makes a useful record. Comparing a scan taken today with one from two years ago shows tooth wear, gum recession and drift far more clearly than memory or notes.

fields.label: Paragraph
fields.value: We still use conventional impressions in the small number of situations where they give a better result, and we will tell you when that is the case.

fields.label: Small heading
fields.value: 3D cone beam (CBCT) imaging

fields.label: Paragraph
fields.value: Cone beam computed tomography produces a three-dimensional image of the jaw, teeth and surrounding structures.

fields.label: Paragraph
fields.value: There are questions a flat X-ray cannot answer. How much bone width is available for an implant. Exactly where the nerve canal runs. Whether a root sits against the sinus. How many canals a molar has and what shape they are. Where an unerupted tooth is positioned relative to its neighbours.

fields.label: Paragraph
fields.value: Having that information before starting is what keeps procedures predictable. It is used here mainly for implant planning, for assessing complicated roots before root canal treatment, and for planning surgical extractions.

fields.label: Small heading
fields.value: Radiation, and using it responsibly

fields.label: Paragraph
fields.value: CBCT delivers a higher radiation dose than a standard dental X-ray. That is the reason it is not used routinely.

fields.label: Paragraph
fields.value: A scan is taken where there is a specific clinical question that a two-dimensional image cannot answer, and where the answer will change what we do. Dr Meg will explain what she is looking for and why before any scan is taken. Where a standard X-ray will do the job, that is what we take.

fields.label: Small heading
fields.value: Seeing what we see

fields.label: Paragraph
fields.value: Both scans display on screen, and you are welcome to look. Most people find a decision easier to make when they can see the problem rather than being told about it.

fields.label: Heading
fields.value: Frequently asked questions

fields.label: Button words
fields.value: Does the scan hurt?

fields.label: Paragraph
fields.value: No. The intra-oral scanner simply passes over the teeth. A CBCT scan involves sitting or standing still for under a minute and nothing touches you.

fields.label: Button words
fields.value: Is a digital scan more accurate than an impression?

fields.label: Paragraph
fields.value: For most restorative work a well-taken digital scan gives an excellent result and removes the discomfort of putty. In a small number of situations a conventional impression remains the better option, and we will use one where that is the case.

fields.label: Button words
fields.value: Why do I need a 3D scan rather than a normal X-ray?

fields.label: Paragraph
fields.value: Because some questions cannot be answered in two dimensions — bone width, nerve position, root anatomy. Where a standard X-ray answers the question, we take one instead.

fields.label: Button words
fields.value: Is CBCT safe?

fields.label: Paragraph
fields.value: It uses a higher dose than a standard dental X-ray, which is why it is taken only where clinically justified. The reason for any scan is explained to you first.

fields.label: Button words
fields.value: Can I have a scan if I am pregnant?

fields.label: Paragraph
fields.value: Tell us before any imaging. Non-urgent radiography is generally deferred during pregnancy, and we will discuss timing with you.

fields.label: Button words
fields.value: Can I get a copy of my scans?

fields.label: Paragraph
fields.value: Yes. Records can be provided to you or sent to another practitioner on request.
